title: The Moment the Mind Became Measurable
author: Science of Explanation
summary: The Science of Explanation newsletter traces how Claude Shannon's 1948 mathematical theory of information made the human mind measurable for the first time. Shannon, a mathematician working on long-distance communication problems, defined information as the resolution of uncertainty and developed a formula -- Information = log2(1/probability) -- that quantified any signal's information content in 'bits.' The less probable a signal, the more information it carries. This gave psychologists a ruler. British psychologist William Hick demonstrated in 1952 that reaction times increased by a fixed amount each time the number of stimulus choices doubled -- precisely matching the bit-by-bit structure of Shannon's formula. The mind was processing information at a measurable rate in bits per millisecond, just as speed is measured in miles per hour. Shannon's contribution launched information theory, computer science, and cognitive science, and established 'the Magna Carta of the information age.'
points: * Shannon defined information as the resolution of uncertainty -- not meaning or content, but the mathematical quantity that transforms an uncertain state into a resolved one. * His formula, Information = log2(1/probability), means surprising signals carry more information than expected ones: rain in Seattle carries less information than snow in Miami in July. * Shannon introduced 'bits' as the unit of information, enabling rigorous measurement of channel capacity, error correction, and compression. * Psychologist William Hick's 1952 reaction-time experiment showed that each doubling of stimulus choices added the same fixed reaction time -- exactly one bit of uncertainty -- confirming that the mind processes information at a measurable rate. * Shannon's work gave cognitive scientists a formal language for thinking about the mind as an information-processing system, directly connecting engineering and psychology.
quotes: Probably the most basic idea in science is measurement. You cannot understand or manipulate something reliably without data.
To him, information exists when there is uncertainty that needs to be resolved.
The genius of Shannon's work is finding a calculation that measures how much information any signal carries, based on its probability.
Once information became measurable, the mind itself became scientifically measurable in a new way.
Each doubling adds one bit. And each additional bit adds the same fixed amount of reaction time. The mind was processing information at a measurable rate, in bits per millisecond.
Shannon gave psychologists a formal language for thinking about the mind as an information-processing system.
